1.q: A product sells for $40. Product plus shipping costs $14 and payment fees are $1.46. What's the break-even ad cost per sale (CPA)?
1.why: Break-even CPA equals gross margin: $40 − $14 − $1.46 = $24.54. Spend less than that per sale on ads and you profit.

1.q: Using the same product, what's the break-even ROAS?
1.why: Break-even ROAS = price ÷ gross margin = $40 ÷ $24.54 ≈ 1.63. Any ROAS above that is profitable before fixed costs.

1.q: Why are products under about $25 hard to sell profitably with paid ads?
o: Ad platforms don't allow cheap products
Ad costs per sale stay similar, but there's much less margin to pay for them
Shopify charges higher fees on cheap products
1.why: Getting a sale costs roughly the same whatever the price, so a low price leaves very little margin to cover the ad cost.

1.q: In Canada, when must a sole proprietor register for GST/HST?
o: As soon as they make their first sale
When taxable sales pass $30,000 over four consecutive calendar quarters
When sales pass $100,000 in one year
1.why: That's the small supplier threshold. You can register earlier voluntarily, and should confirm the details with an accountant.

1.q: Which niche fits the course's criteria best?
o: Phone cases, because demand is huge
Home pet grooming: passionate owners, $25–$80 products, easy to demo
1.why: Clothing brings sizing returns, supplements bring health-claim risk, and phone cases are cheap and crowded. Pet grooming scores well on every criterion.

1.q: How much of a starting budget should go to testing ads?
o: Nothing until the store has sales
Exactly half, with half on samples
1.why: Ad tests are how you learn what sells, so most of your first budget is 'tuition' spent on testing.

2.q: Which is the strongest sign that a product really sells?
o: A video with a lot of likes
Several different stores running ads for it for 30+ days
A friend says they'd buy it
2.why: Nobody keeps paying for an ad that loses money. Several advertisers running for a month or more is real evidence.

2.q: Where do you check how long a competitor's ad has been running?
o: The 'Started running on' date in the Meta Ad Library
2.why: The Meta Ad Library is free and shows each ad's start date and how many versions are running.

2.q: Which reviews tell you the most about a product's weaknesses?
2.why: 5-star reviews are vague and 1-star reviews are often about shipping. 3-star reviewers explain exactly what almost worked.

2.q: On Google Trends, a product's interest spikes sharply and then falls. How should you treat it?
o: As a trend or seasonal product: it can make money quickly, but plan your exit
As not worth testing at all
2.why: Spiky interest means a trend or season. Launch a seasonal product 4–6 weeks before its peak and don't build your whole store on it.

2.q: What's a strong mix for your three test products?
o: The three cheapest products you can find
One evergreen, one seasonal or trending, one higher-priced or bundle product
Three products from three unrelated niches
2.why: The mix spreads risk and gives you a product to raise average order value, while staying in one niche for one customer.

3.q: Which shipping should you always use?
3.why: Untracked parcels lead to refund disputes you can't win, and customers expect a tracking link.

3.q: How do you calculate your delivery promise?
o: Processing time + shipping time + about 2 days of buffer
Always 3–5 days, because customers expect it
3.why: Under-promise and over-deliver. Customers mind being misled far more than they mind waiting.

3.q: Why ask suppliers to ship without invoices or promotional material?
o: So customers don't see supplier prices or another brand in their parcel
3.why: A supplier's price tag or flyer in the box breaks your brand and invites refund requests.

3.q: A customer receives a damaged item that cost you $8. What does the course usually recommend?
o: Ask them to ship it back to the supplier in China
Refuse, because shipping damage isn't your fault
Refund or reship without asking for it back
3.why: For low-cost items, sending them back costs more than the item. Refund or reship, then claim from the supplier.

3.q: What should you do before listing a product for sale?
o: Order a sample and test it yourself
Wait for the first customer to report problems
3.why: Samples show real quality, packaging and delivery time, and give you footage for ads.

4.q: What should a product page's first image show?
o: The product on a white background
4.why: People buy the outcome, not the object. Show it working.

4.q: Which of these is NOT allowed?
o: Asking for real reviews 14 days after delivery
Importing reviews copied from another store
Using real photos of your samples
4.why: Copied or fake reviews are deceptive marketing. Collect real ones from your own customers.

4.q: Why set your payment statement descriptor to your store name?
o: Customers recognise the charge, which prevents chargebacks
4.why: An unrecognised charge on a bank statement is a common reason customers file a chargeback.

4.q: Which offer raises average order value?
4.why: Quantity breaks and bundles raise the order value while ad cost per order stays about the same.

4.q: What should you do right before launching?
o: Install as many apps as possible
Place a full test order and check emails, shipping rates and the supplier app
4.why: The test order catches broken checkouts, wrong shipping text and missing emails before real customers do.

5.q: In a 30-second ad, what are the first 0–3 seconds for?
5.why: Most viewers decide in the first 1–3 seconds. Write ten hooks for every ad you film.

5.q: An ad has spent 1× your break-even CPA with no add-to-carts and a 0.6% CTR. What do you do?
o: Kill it and test a new hook
5.why: Low CTR means the creative isn't stopping people. The kill rules say stop it and test a new hook.

5.q: An ad set has had a CPA below break-even for 3+ days and several purchases. How do you scale it?
o: Raise the budget about 20% every 48 hours
Turn it off to reset learning
Duplicate it into ten ad sets at once
5.why: Big jumps reset the platform's learning. Steady increases keep the cost per sale stable.

5.q: An ad gets a good CTR and plenty of clicks, but very few add-to-carts. What's the most likely problem?
o: The page or price doesn't match the ad's promise
5.why: People are interested enough to click, so the ad works. The page loses them.

5.q: When should the first abandoned-checkout email go out?
5.why: An hour later the buyer is still thinking about it, without feeling chased.

5.q: What does Canada's anti-spam law (CASL) require for marketing emails?
o: Consent, sender identification and an easy unsubscribe
5.why: Consent first, a clear identity, and a working unsubscribe in every email.

6.q: A parcel's tracking hasn't updated for 10+ days. What do you do?
o: Tell the customer it's out of your hands
Ask the customer to contact the carrier
Reship or refund, then claim from the supplier
6.why: Protect the customer relationship first, then recover the cost from your supplier.

6.why: Customers who get quick, kind answers come to you instead of their bank.

6.q: Which pattern usually means creative fatigue?
o: Frequency rising above 3–4 while CTR drops
6.why: The same people are seeing the same ad too often. You need new creatives, not new audiences.

6.why: Blended ROAS includes email sales and returning customers, so it shows whether the whole business is profitable.

6.q: Until an accountant gives you a better number, how much profit should you set aside for tax?
6.why: Setting aside 25–30% avoids a painful surprise at tax time.
